Encryption stops your Internet provider, or the public Wi-Fi you are on, from seeing the list of services your phone contacts, a list that says a lot about you.

DNS is the Internet\'s directory: it turns a site name, like example.org, into the address your phone connects to.

You turn it on once in the settings, and it protects every app on the phone.
It is not a VPN: it does not hide your IP address and does not make your browsing anonymous. The sites you visit still see your address.

Find the apps you no longer use
Android can tell VYLIA when each app was last opened. This usage access is read on your phone only and never leaves it. You can withdraw it at any time in the same screen.

Switching apps is often the most radical way to protect your data, but it is not always possible. Your bank, public services, the tool your employer requires or the messaging app your friends and family use usually have no equivalent.

That is why the approach starts by reducing the risk of the apps you keep: removing needless permissions, deleting forgotten apps, blocking ad tracking. That is what the Reduce tab is for. Only then, when an alternative exists, does switching become worthwhile: choose a category below to see two or three of them.

Some people go further and adopt a fully « de-Googled » phone, one that works without Google services. That path calls for compromises not everyone is ready to make, and it is not VYLIA\'s: our approach is to reduce your exposure while you keep your phone and your usual apps.
Installing an alternative earns the Good swap trophy.

These apps come from AlternativeTo, a site where people recommend alternatives to one another. In each category, VYLIA keeps the free apps that users like most, available on Android, and opens their Google Play page (or F-Droid if there is none). It reflects popularity, not an audit: their score appears in VYLIA once you install them.
Two ways to cut ad tracking
Before contacting a tracker\'s server, an app asks for its address (a DNS request). Refusing to answer that request stops the data from being sent, for every app at once. Two tools can do it:

• VYLIA Shield: the filtering is done on the phone, with VYLIA\'s lists. One switch, a choice between web and mobile filtering, a pause, and a live counter. It uses a local VPN (Android allows only one VPN at a time) and does not encrypt the requests it lets through.

• Private DNS: your requests are encrypted and sent to a service you choose, set once in Android\'s settings, with no VPN. It only blocks trackers if that service filters them (NextDNS can, Quad9 does not), and the service sees your requests.

Use one or the other: when private DNS is set to a service, Android sends it the requests directly and the Shield sees none of them. To block trackers simply, choose the Shield; to also encrypt your requests, choose a private DNS that filters (NextDNS).
Blocks the tracking requests of all your apps, right on the phone.
Stopped: another VPN took over. Android only allows one at a time.
Could not start. Try again; if it keeps failing, check the VPN screen in Android settings.

How it works: VYLIA creates a VPN on the phone itself. Only DNS requests (the Internet\'s directory) go through it: those for known tracking servers are refused, the others go on to your network\'s usual DNS. Nothing is sent to a VYLIA server, and the rest of your traffic does not go through VYLIA.
Private DNS is set to %1$s: Android then sends its requests straight to that service and the Shield sees none of them. Choose one or the other: to use the Shield, set private DNS back to Automatic.
Another VPN is on: turning on the Shield will replace it.
Limits: apps that encrypt their own DNS (some browsers) bypass the Shield, and blocking a tracker can occasionally break a feature: if an app misbehaves, turn the Shield off.

To keep it on after a restart, turn on “Always-on VPN” for VYLIA in Android\'s VPN settings, but leave “Block connections without VPN” off: the Shield only carries DNS, so that option would cut off the Internet.
Ads and trackers of websites, including those opened inside apps, and audience measurement of apps (Firebase, Amplitude, Adjust…). It rarely bothers apps or games.
Ad networks of apps and games (AppLovin, Unity Ads, ironSource, Google AdMob…): their ads and the profile they build of you are blocked, but so are rewarded videos (in games, for example).
You play a lot? Turn off mobile filtering: rewarded videos work and web filtering carries on. Networks that serve both apps and websites (Google AdMob, DoubleClick) then go through too.
Paused until %1$s: nothing is blocked, then the Shield resumes by itself.

Some features depend on a server the Shield blocks. A pause lets everything through for the time you choose with − and + (5 minutes to 2 hours), then protection resumes without you having to think about it, unlike turning the Shield off.

• A rewarded video, in a game for example (extra life, bonus), spins without loading: it is an ad, served by the networks the Shield blocks. For a whole gaming session, choose the duration (60 min…), or turn off mobile filtering.
• A link in an email, a newsletter or an ad does not open: it often goes through a click-tracking server before reaching the site.
• A promo code, cashback or referral is not credited: these offers rely on tracking to know where you came from.
• A sponsored result, in a search engine or a shopping app, leads nowhere: it goes through the ad network first.
• An app shows an error, a blank page or keeps loading: if the pause fixes it, the Shield was the cause, and the latest blocks show which server.
Nothing is counted during the pause: the trackers contacted then are not blocked.

resources.string: How the permissions and trackers of each app shape its score and its badges, and what they mean for your privacy.
The main families of trackers, what they do with your data and the most common ones. A tracker can belong to several families: the most serious one counts in the score.
Tap a permission to see what it allows, why it is sensitive and how it is granted.
The Privacy Score at a glance

Every app starts with %1$d points. It loses points for the permissions it requests and the trackers it embeds, and spying capabilities can cap its score. Everything is computed on your phone, offline.

The permission penalty is not the same for every app: it depends on what the app is for. GPS costs nothing to a navigation app, which needs it, but costs a lot to a game, which has no reason to use it (details in 1 and 3 below).
The caps keep a single aspect from crushing everything: an app never loses more than %1$d points for its permissions nor more than %2$d for its trackers.
The grade and its risk level
A “%1$s” after the grade (e.g. %2$s) marks a provisional score: the trackers could not be analysed yet.
Each counted permission has a weight according to its severity: from %1$d (%2$s) to %3$d (%4$s). This weight is then adjusted by two questions.
Is it related to what the app does? (context)
Justified (×%1$s): needed for the feature, e.g. GPS for a navigation app.
Unexpected (×%1$s): no obvious link with the app\'s category.
Forbidden (×%1$s): no justification at all, e.g. contacts for a game.
A granted permission counts in full. A permission that is only declared (the app plans for it but you have not accepted it) counts ×%1$s: it remains a sign of intent.
Precise location weighs %1$d. Granted to a navigation app, where it is justified: %1$d × %2$s = 0 points lost. Granted to a game, where it is forbidden: %1$d × %3$s = %4$s points lost.
Capabilities that depend on an access

Some permissions are useless on their own. Running the microphone, camera or location in the background requires that access to be granted first; until then they count ×%1$s. Screen capture needs your consent every time, so it always counts ×%1$s.
Ad targeting permissions (advertising ID, Android\'s ad services) are not counted here: advertising is already penalised through the trackers.
Precise and approximate location count only once (the heavier one).
Photos, videos, audio and legacy file access count only once.
For SMS, the heaviest counts in full, the others at half weight.
Background location, classic or through a foreground service, counts only once.
For Health Connect data, only the most sensitive tier counts.
Legacy file access only counts for apps built for Android 12 or earlier: beyond that, Android ignores it.

A tracker is a piece of code supplied by another company (often an ad network) and built into the app. It collects information about you and sends it to its own servers, in addition to the app\'s publisher.

VYLIA spots them by looking for their signatures in each app\'s code, using the public Exodus Privacy database. Each tracker costs points according to what it does; a tracker with several uses counts as the most serious one.
This is where advertising is counted: ad and profiling trackers are the heaviest. Ad targeting permissions are therefore not counted a second time.
What each category does, with examples, in the Trackers tab.
Trackers cannot cost more than %1$d points in total.
If the analysis could not be done
Until the analysis is done (or if the app could not be read), a flat %1$d points are deducted and the grade carries a “%2$s”.
Detection relies on known code names. A hidden (obfuscated) or very recent tracker can go unnoticed: “no tracker detected” is not an absolute guarantee.

What is “justified” depends on what the app does: the microphone is normal for Shazam, not for a calculator. VYLIA puts each app into one of %1$d categories, based on a list of known apps or, failing that, the category declared by the publisher.
An “Uncategorised” app gets no special treatment: every sensitive permission is considered unexpected.

Some combinations are typical of spyware: reading what you type, recording in the background, hiding its icon with sensitive accesses, reading the screen and drawing over other apps. They describe what an app CAN do, not what it does, but they cap its score:
Badges sum up at a glance what an app does well and what deserves your attention. They do not change the score. Every badge and its rule are in the Badges tab.
Few or no sensitive permissions, and they serve the app\'s purpose; no trackers, or almost none.
A few tolerated permissions or a small number of trackers, often analytics or crash reporting.
Permissions unrelated to the app\'s purpose, or several trackers including advertising ones. Keep an eye on it.
Typically many advertising or profiling trackers, often with intrusive permissions. Look for an alternative.
Massive data collection. Replace it if you can.
Below %1$d, an app necessarily combines intrusive permissions (more than %2$d points) and significant trackers (more than %3$d points).
Permissions alone (capped at %1$d) cannot bring an app below %2$d: trackers necessarily weigh in, more than %3$d points.
Permissions alone (capped at %1$d) cannot bring an app below %2$d: trackers necessarily weigh in.

Badges sum up what an app does well and what deserves your attention, without changing its score. A card shows at most three, the most important first. Each rule below is read from the rules in force.

its trackers cover at least %1$d of: %2$s.
a good-practice badge for both permissions and trackers, and no point of attention.
a red badge on both the permissions or security side and the trackers side.
at least %1$d of these, %2$s for its category%3$s: %4$s.

The Internet is only used when you ask for it: to update the tracker database (the public Exodus Privacy list) or the list of private DNS services (published with VYLIA\'s source code). Nothing about your apps is sent.
Install alerts and background scans are off by default. Once turned on, they run on the phone only, scheduled by Android.

To analyse your apps, VYLIA needs the list of installed apps (QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES): without it, there is nothing to audit. It owns this: VYLIA scores itself with the same rules as every other app, and this permission costs it points. Its page is in Scan, like the others.
Results stay on the phone. You can export, import or delete them at any time (Settings › Data management), and share your rewards from the Act tab.
